name: System on Chip

claims.claim_text: Multi-die packaging lets a vendor sell what looks like a single chip: dies that cannot be built on one piece of silicon, such as a large flash array alongside a processor, are stacked or flipped together inside one package, removing the external memory chip from the bill of materials.
claims.quote_verbatim: instead of you requiring an extra flash memory chip, it's, you know, this massive amount of flash memory is built into the one chip. And the way they do it, they can't fit it on the single die. So they just do it as separate dies.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Dave Is Back And Blogging!

claims.claim_text: Putting a co-processor and its accelerators on a single die is favourable for power because unused blocks can be shut off, and it also lets an existing platform be extended by dropping a co-processor alongside the main application processor rather than redesigning around a new one.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's good for power. It means that, you know, if you've got an old mobile phone platform, you can drop a co-processor in
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eben Upton - Morbus Moilsome MakerFaire

claims.claim_text: An individual IP block licensed into a larger system-on-chip can carry documentation on the scale of a printed phone book, because every configurable register of the block is exposed to the integrator.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you printed out the data sheet, would be the size of a small phone book because of all the registers
claims.speaker: Alan Wolke
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Alan Wolke (Re-broadcast)

claims.claim_text: Application processors integrate memory, graphics processing and DSP blocks into a single-chip solution, with the memory die packaged on top of the processor die rather than placed separately on the board.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's got the memory, you know, flipped on top of it. It's got like graphics processes and stuff built in
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Open Source RC & Modelsource - Facinorous Financial Foulness

claims.claim_text: Because a design becomes a handful of large processor, FPGA or system-on-chip packages joined by modular blocks rather than hundreds of small logic packages, autorouting has lost the role it had when boards carried rows of 74-series TTL in DIP.
claims.quote_verbatim: So often a design these days is just all these little modular blocks joining into one big huge chip or a couple of big huge processor or FPGA chips
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Intel, EPA & Brown Field - Google's Ground Gurgitation

claims.claim_text: A Bluetooth system-on-chip of the early 2010s put an ARM core, SRAM, baseband processing, encoding and the radio circuitry on one die, so a sensor node needed little beyond the chip itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's got SRAM on it. It's got baseband type stuff. It's got encoding. It's got radio circuitry
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Firmware, Netburner and Semiconductors - Chris's Capitalism Colloquy

claims.claim_text: An early-2010s Bluetooth Low Energy system-on-chip drew about 3.8 milliamps in both receive and transmit.
claims.quote_verbatim: it needs 3.8 milliamps for receiving and TX
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Firmware, Netburner and Semiconductors - Chris's Capitalism Colloquy

claims.claim_text: The Xilinx Zynq combined a dual-core 1 GHz ARM Cortex-A9 processor with FPGA fabric on one die, and higher models added hard-logic DDR2 and DDR3 memory controllers and high-speed serial transceivers.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a dual, it's a dual ARM one gig processor, A9 processor
claims.episode_title: Tesla, FPGAs and DigiKey - Zesty Zippy Zynq

claims.claim_text: Supplying a system-on-chip can dominate the board physically: with a separate inductor required per rail, the power supply occupies more area than the processor, and the inductors alone can be larger than the FPGA they feed, while adding cost and efficiency loss.
claims.quote_verbatim: The power supply is bigger than the system on chip. Just the inductors alone can be bigger than the entire FPGA.
claims.episode_title: Tesla, FPGAs and DigiKey - Zesty Zippy Zynq

claims.claim_text: Moving from a single-board computer to a design with the system-on-chip mounted directly on one's own board is a large discontinuity in skill, which is why vendors offer compute modules as an intermediate step; the alternative is going straight to a high-speed DDR3 layout.
claims.quote_verbatim: without needing, figuring out how to get into the world of like, uh, you know, putting an SOC chip onto a board themselves
claims.speaker: Matt Richardson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Richardson - Raspberry Risorgimento Regent

claims.claim_text: A chip vendor's own assessment in the mid-2010s was that a one-gigahertz system-on-chip selling for one dollar was not achievable at the time, whatever a board price built on that assumption implied.
claims.quote_verbatim: a one gigahertz system on chip that costs a dollar is just not possible
claims.episode_title: Consolidate All The Things - Zonked Zelotic Zaitech

claims.claim_text: For application-specific system-on-chips serving a narrow end product, only two or three manufacturers may make the part, and the firmware is commonly written by the chip manufacturer to a settings list supplied by the equipment maker rather than by the equipment maker itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'll get the manufacturer of that cool SOC to do it for me, and I'll tell them what settings I want
claims.speaker: Dafydd Roche
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Dafydd Roche

claims.claim_text: Evaluation modules and tooling quality are decisive for parts that require firmware work, and for high-performance parts the vendor must publish example layouts showing how the board is to be laid out.
claims.quote_verbatim: Good tools, good EVMs are very important for parts where there's some firmware to be done.
claims.speaker: Dafydd Roche
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Dafydd Roche

claims.claim_text: System-on-chip power rails are typically variable-voltage rather than fixed, because the supply voltage is lowered together with the clock frequency to obtain the best power efficiency; the external supply therefore has to be a variable source.
claims.quote_verbatim: the power supplies are variable voltage so they can get the best power efficiency
claims.episode_title: An Interview with David Kronstein (Tesla500)

claims.claim_text: Security assumptions are lost along the system-on-chip supply chain: a silicon vendor may reasonably assume that anyone with physical access to the chip can reprogram it, but that assumption is not passed on to the board maker, the OEM that badges the board, or the software vendor above them.
claims.quote_verbatim: the SOC vendor might think like anybody who has physical access to this SOC can reprogram it. And that's a valid assumption. The problem is they don't pass that along.
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe FitzPatrick

claims.claim_text: Pairing a processor with FPGA fabric in one device suits systems where a very high-bandwidth data path must be managed by logic that does not itself need high bandwidth, such as a telecoms base station routing packet transactions; the cost of the processor is absorbed into the fabric rather than paid separately.
claims.quote_verbatim: the data pipe needed to be very high bandwidth. But the management of that data pipe didn't need to be so high bandwidth
claims.speaker: Kieran O'Leary
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Kieran O'Leary

claims.claim_text: Integration on FPGA-based system-on-chips extended to RF: Xilinx released an RF SoC with multiple RF DACs and ADCs integrated onto the die, allowing a software-defined radio or radar system, including its DSP, to be built on one chip.
claims.quote_verbatim: Xilinx brought out an RF SOC, which is quite novel, that had an RF, you know, or multiple RF DACs and ADCs integrated into the package
claims.speaker: Kieran O'Leary
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Kieran O'Leary

claims.claim_text: When the processor cores and the programmable fabric sit on the same die, communication bandwidth between them is not a design constraint, because the link is internal rather than a serialised off-chip interface.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's, it's just like a very tightly integrated SOC. So communication bandwidth is never an issue between the FPGA and the ARM cores
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan Cousins

claims.claim_text: Even on a tightly integrated device, a signal path that runs from a custom peripheral in the fabric to a bare-metal core and up to a Linux core and back consumes significant time, so buffer sizes and how often the operating system services the interface have to be sized for the case where the call is late or never arrives.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like that's still a decent amount of timing to get all the way up and all the way back down.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan Cousins

claims.claim_text: In a soft system-on-chip built on FPGA fabric the number of CPU cores can be a single Verilog parameter, but beyond a certain count added cores stop helping because the shared memory bus becomes the constraint and the CPUs wait on each other.
claims.quote_verbatim: above a certain count, it doesn't make sense because the memory bus gets so constrained that all the CPUs are waiting on each other
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg
claims.episode_title: Stories from Supercon 2019

claims.claim_text: Designing a system-on-chip of any reasonable size costs on the order of 50 to 100 million dollars even when a large proportion of the design is assembled from pre-built IP blocks.
claims.quote_verbatim: designing an soc is really expensive so even if you're using a lot of pre-built blocks it's still probably a 50 100 million dollar endeavor
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Yield falls as die area grows, because a fixed density of wafer defects removes a larger fraction of big dies; this is why cost-down revisions shrink the die, which lowers price and raises yield at once.
claims.quote_verbatim: as your chip gets bigger your yield goes down
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Integrating more of a system onto one piece of silicon trades away interoperability: the more functions are absorbed into the chip, the less able the system designer is to swap an individual part out, and chip design remains far less accessible than board design.
claims.quote_verbatim: why not just put all the silicon together then but then you start to lose the interoperability
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Chiplet integration is offered as an alternative to a monolithic system-on-chip built on one process node, with time to market as the claimed advantage: production samples in months rather than the quarters or years a monolithic part requires.
claims.quote_verbatim: the advantage of chiplet integration compared to monolithic system on a chip would be time to market
claims.speaker: Ming Zhang
claims.episode_title: Discussing Chiplets with Ming Zhang

claims.claim_text: A system-on-chip vendor's configuration interface is aimed at the system designer rather than the chip designer, letting the buyer specify how much RAM and how many converters are wanted, which yields far more combinations than the fixed option table of a microcontroller family.
claims.quote_verbatim: So this is an interface. Who's using that interface? Not the chip designer. Is a system designer.
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: The Broadcom part at the centre of the early Raspberry Pi was designed as a multimedia co-processor to sit alongside a phone's main SoC; an ARM core was grafted onto it, which turned it into a small system-on-chip capable of running Linux, and it was inexpensive because phone makers do not pay much for silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's kind of like a little system on a chip that could run Linux
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: Embedded Hardware with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: With RISC-V the instruction set architecture is fixed by a ratified specification, but the microarchitecture, the number of cores, how those cores communicate and what I/O goes on the chip are all left to the implementer, so implementations of the same ISA vary widely.
claims.quote_verbatim: the micro architectural implementation or how many cores you're going to have or how these cores are going to talk to each other, what kind of IO are you going to put in a chip? All of this is up to you.
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: A multi-core Linux-capable RISC-V system-on-chip can be fitted into an FPGA of roughly 35,000 LUTs or fewer, rather than requiring a top-end device.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can put a multi-core Linux capable SOC into your FPGA. And I'm not talking about like a huge VU19 FPGA. I'm talking about something that has, you know, 35K LUTs or less
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Teams take the IP cores bundled with a vendor tool chain because building the equivalent from scratch is about twice the work, so open alternatives only displace vendor IP where they are already good enough to use in practice.
claims.quote_verbatim: building this from scratch is twice the work that just grabbing Silenx IP
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: A hard requirement such as a large FPGA with hard processor cores narrows the choice to one or two devices, and the vendor tool chain then comes with the device; replacing a tool chain is not something a project takes on against a deadline.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't just turn around and like use something smaller because of the, you know, the hardware requirements and you aren't going to go and write, you know, try and blow up a tool chain when you have a deadline
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: A system-in-package keeps the microcontroller and the radio transceiver as separate dies in one package, whereas the succeeding part licenses the transceiver design and combines everything onto a single die, giving more integration and a smaller footprint.
claims.quote_verbatim: Microcontroller and the transceiver was different dye, but this one combines everything into one dye.
claims.episode_title: Generic Nodes with Orkhan Amiraslanov

claims.claim_text: During the semiconductor shortage the lead time on commodity microcontrollers was long enough that designing a custom RISC-V system-on-chip and having it fabricated would have been quicker than waiting for STM32 parts to arrive.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was a time when we were, would have been quicker to have designed your own RISC-V SOC and had it fabricated than wait for some STM32s to come in
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: The case for a custom chip is normally a system-on-chip case rather than a processor case: outside a learning exercise there is little reason to design a new processor core when off-the-shelf RISC-V cores are available, and the motivation is custom peripherals, a particular feature set or a custom instruction.
claims.quote_verbatim: You should just use one of the many RISC-V processes that are like available off the shelf.
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: System-on-chip selection can be driven by the display interface rather than by compute: a part was chosen for a head-mounted design because it offered both MIPI DSI and LVDS outputs matching the display in use, alongside on-chip H.264 and H.265 encode and decode.
claims.quote_verbatim: It has MIPI DSI outputs. It also has LVDS outputs, which were important for the display I was using at that point.
claims.speaker: Aedan Cullen
claims.episode_title: Building AR Headsets with Aedan Cullen

claims.claim_text: Packaging the same die with integrated DDR2 memory produces a variant part that removes the external memory and its high-speed routing from the board, which is what makes a miniaturised design low cost and straightforward to lay out.
claims.quote_verbatim: They also package it with integrated DDR2 in that D1S package
claims.speaker: Aedan Cullen
claims.episode_title: Building AR Headsets with Aedan Cullen

claims.claim_text: Many blocks inside a system-on-chip are designed by companies other than the chip maker and licensed in, so the display controller or similar subsystem in one vendor's SoC may be the same IP family found in another's.
claims.quote_verbatim: you find that with a lot of blocks in these SOCs. You know, they're designed by other companies other than the SOC maker, and then they get dropped in.
claims.speaker: Aedan Cullen
claims.episode_title: Building AR Headsets with Aedan Cullen

claims.claim_text: Stacking bare memory and storage dice on top of the system-on-chip requires interposer-level design rules of roughly 10 to 20 microns line and space, which conventional PCB processes cannot achieve.
claims.quote_verbatim: So 10, 20 microns space width and tracing, standard PCB won't cut it in this case.
claims.speaker: Lukas Henkel
claims.episode_title: Compact High Speed Design with Lukas Henkel

claims.claim_text: Advanced integration steps such as embedded components and stacked bare dice are technically available but only rational at volume, since the non-recurring engineering and time investment have to be recovered across a common enough use case.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to get enough volume to actually make that a reality so that it's worth that NRE
claims.speaker: Lukas Henkel
claims.episode_title: Compact High Speed Design with Lukas Henkel

claims.claim_text: An eMCP package combining 4 GB of LPDDR4X with 64 GB of eMMC is dominated by the memory dice themselves, with the moulding accounting for perhaps 10 to 20 percent of the package volume, so the only remaining path to a smaller module is stacking the memory onto the system-on-chip.
claims.quote_verbatim: 4 gigabytes of LPDDR4X and 64 gigabytes of MMC and it's just memory dice are large
claims.speaker: Lukas Henkel
claims.episode_title: Compact High Speed Design with Lukas Henkel

claims.claim_text: On-chip SRAM is the practical limit on how much a small custom die can do, which is what separates a microcontroller from a microprocessor design: memory has to be placed off chip once the on-die SRAM runs out.
claims.quote_verbatim: limitations are usually going to be like onboard SRAM. You know, you're going to go off chip for a lot of this stuff
claims.episode_title: Building wafer.space with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: A Linux-capable system-on-chip has been taped out on a 130 nm shuttle by a single part-time developer with no prior chip design experience, and it boots an unmodified upstream Linux kernel with no board support package required.
claims.quote_verbatim: I want this to boot mainstream upstream Linux kernel. You don't need some board support package or anything.
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Building wafer.space with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Before system-on-chip parts existed for the application, first-generation DVD players were built from large amounts of non-specialised discrete circuitry, reaching a single board of roughly 10 by 12 inches, and the product retailed for over a thousand early-1990s dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: There was a large amount of discrete circuitry in it, not specialized circuitry, not system on a chip mentality.
claims.episode_title: Applied Embedded Electronics with Jerry Twomey
